items.name: Severe-bleeding control: tourniquet and dressings
items.need: Life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg can kill before an ambulance arrives, and a real tourniquet plus a pressure dressing lets a bystander stop it.
items.how_to_choose: Buy a windlass tourniquet recommended by the Committee on Tactical Combat Casualty Care (CoTCCC), such as the C-A-T Gen 7, and buy it from the maker's distributor or the Stop the Bleed store, never from a marketplace seller. A kit that adds hemostatic gauze, a trauma dressing, gloves and shears is worth the extra cost. Then take a Stop the Bleed class: the kit is of little use without practice.

qty.note: One per household to start. Add one per bag if you can.

items.already_own: Only trust a tourniquet you can trace to an authorized seller. If yours came from a marketplace listing, a multi-pack, or cost well under $25, replace it. Practice on a training device, not the one kept for real use: a tourniquet that has been used for practice should be kept for practice only.

safety_notes.text: The American College of Surgeons Stop the Bleed course teaches three actions for severe bleeding: apply direct pressure with your hands, pack the wound, and apply a tourniquet. The course is for anyone old enough to understand it. In-person classes have an instructor check your technique, and a virtual course is also offered.
safety_notes.source_name: American College of Surgeons Stop the Bleed

safety_notes.text: The Stop the Bleed program lists the standard contents of its kits: a C-A-T tourniquet, compressed or hemostatic gauze, an emergency trauma dressing, trauma shears, a marker, gloves and bleeding-control instructions. It sells kits through its own store.
safety_notes.source_name: American College of Surgeons Stop the Bleed

safety_notes.text: The C-A-T's US distributor says the real tourniquets are single-use devices and sells a blue trainer that can be used over and over in training, colored blue to tell it apart from the ones kept for real use. Practice on a training device, not the one kept for real use, and keep a fresh one ready for an emergency.
safety_notes.source_title: What is the difference between the colors of the CAT

safety_notes.text: The blue C-A-T trainer is a working Gen 7 tourniquet made for hands-on training and practice; its color marks it as a training device, separate from personal, life-saving ones.

item_flags: Counterfeit tourniquets are common. North American Rescue, the US distributor of the C-A-T, says large numbers of fake C-A-Ts made in China have reached first responders and failed or broken when used. It and the maker obtained a US International Trade Commission general exclusion order so that Customs can seize imports that look like a C-A-T. Genuine C-A-Ts are made only in the United States.
C-A-T Resources describes itself as the inventor and exclusive manufacturer of the C-A-T and names North American Rescue as its United States distributor.

Do not buy tourniquets or hemostatic gauze from third-party marketplace sellers (Amazon Marketplace, eBay, Temu and similar). Buy from North American Rescue, the Stop the Bleed store, or another dealer the maker names.
The Prepared's tourniquet review gives the same warning: if it looks like a C-A-T but does not come from North American Rescue, or costs under $25, do not buy it.
The blue C-A-T is a training device. Do not carry it as your real tourniquet, and do not practice with the real one.

items.name: N95 respirators
items.need: A NIOSH-approved N95 filters wildfire smoke, building dust and airborne germs in a way that cloth and surgical masks do not.
items.how_to_choose: Buy only NIOSH-approved respirators with two head straps and a TC-84A approval number printed on them, from a known retailer. Fit matters as much as the filter: try a model before you need it, and pick another shape if it leaks at the edges. Respirators with an exhalation valve are cooler to wear but do not filter the air you breathe out.

qty.note: 6 for each person who can wear one, the same at every level: this site's assumption of 2 a day for 3 smoky days, not an official figure. This site counts adults and teenagers aged 14 or over. No respirator is counted for a child under 14, and none is ever put on a child under 2.

items.already_own: Leftover N95s are fine if they are a NIOSH-approved model, the straps still stretch and the nose foam is intact. Look up the TC number on the NIOSH Certified Equipment List. KN95s and ear-loop masks are not NIOSH approved.

safety_notes.text: A NIOSH-approved N95 is marked with the approval holder's name or logo, the word NIOSH, a TC approval number in the form TC-84A-XXXX, the model number and the filter class (such as N95). A respirator missing any of these is not NIOSH approved. The easiest check is to search the TC number in the NIOSH Certified Equipment List.
The NIOSH Certified Equipment List is the official list of approved respirators. The model and approval number on the product must match the listing.

NIOSH warns about counterfeit and misrepresented respirators. On marketplaces, be wary of listings that insist the product is 'genuine' or 'legitimate', sellers that move between trending products, big price swings, prices too good to be true and claims of unlimited stock during a shortage.

For wildfire smoke, EPA says to use a respirator printed with NIOSH and a filter class such as N95 or P100. Paint masks, dust masks and surgical masks do not prevent smoke inhalation. The respirator must sit tightly over the nose and under the chin with both straps around the head; check the seal each time, because any gap lets smoke in. Take frequent breaks, drink water, and take it off as soon as you can if you feel dizzy or have trouble breathing.
safety_notes.source_title: Strategies to Reduce Exposure Outdoors (Wildfire Smoke and Your Patients' Health)

safety_notes.text: Children: CDC says children aged 2 and older can wear respirators and masks, but NIOSH Approved respirators do not come in sizes suitable for very young children, and smaller sizes may not have been designed or tested for children. FDA says N95s are not designed for children or for people with facial hair. This site counts no respirator for a child under 14 and never puts one on a child under 2; a young child's protection is the clean room.
safety_notes.source_title: Safety Guidelines: Wildfires and Wildfire Smoke

safety_notes.text: FDA says people with chronic breathing or heart conditions should check with a health-care provider before using an N95. N95s are single-use: replace one that is damaged, dirty or hard to breathe through. A surgical mask does not filter very small particles in the air.
safety_notes.source_title: N95 Respirators, Surgical Masks, Face Masks, and Barrier Face Coverings

safety_notes.text: Ready.gov's basic kit list includes a dust mask to help filter contaminated air. A NIOSH-approved N95 is the stronger choice for smoke, per EPA above.

item_flags: Counterfeit and falsely labeled respirators are sold on marketplaces. Buy from the maker's named retailers, a hardware store or a safety supplier, and check the TC number against the NIOSH list.

No NIOSH-approved respirator is sized for very young children. A small adult respirator on a child is not a tested fit. For young children the plan is to keep them in the clean room, out of smoke and dust, not to rely on a mask.

items.need: A whistle carries much farther than a voice and takes little breath, which matters if you are trapped, hurt, or trying to regroup in a crowd.

items.name: Work gloves
items.need: After a blast, quake or storm the streets and stairwells are covered in broken glass and sharp debris, and gloves let you move it, climb over it and open jammed doors without cutting your hands.
items.how_to_choose: Leather or a rated cut-resistant palm is what protects against glass; thin synthetic gloves do not. Where a maker publishes an ANSI/ISEA 105 cut level (A1 to A9), a higher level means more cut resistance. Fit matters: gloves that are too big make you clumsy.

qty.note: One pair per adult, kept in the bag.

items.already_own: Leather gardening or work gloves in good condition are fine. Thin knit, latex or winter gloves are not a substitute.
item_flags: Cut ratings differ a lot between the picks. The Cadillac has a high published ANSI/ISEA 105 cut level (A8). The Standard's published level is A1, the lowest, and the Budget pick has none, so treat both as protection against scrapes and light debris, not as proof against sharp glass edges.
No glove is cut-proof. Pick glass up by the flat faces and do not grip edges.

items.name: Fire-resistant chest for papers at home
items.need: Originals such as birth certificates, passports, deeds and policies are slow to replace, and a fire-rated chest at home gives them a chance of surviving a fire.
items.how_to_choose: Only buy a chest whose maker states a UL fire classification with a time and a temperature, such as 1/2 hour at 1550 F. Prefer one that is also rated for water, because sprinklers and fire hoses soak a home even when the fire is on another floor. Fire chests and safes are heavy, from about 13 lb for the smallest chest here to about 87 lb for the safe, so check the weight and where it will sit before you buy.

qty.note: One per household, kept at home.

items.already_own: A fire chest or safe you already own is good enough if its label names a UL fire classification with a time and a temperature.
item_flags: Many 'fireproof' document bags sold on marketplaces have no independent fire rating at all. Fabric bags described only as 'fire resistant to 2000 F' or 'silicone coated fiberglass' are untested claims. Do not rely on one for originals.
The fire and water ratings below are the maker's own statements.
A half-hour fire rating is modest. Keep copies or scans elsewhere too (see the encrypted USB drive and the document pouch).
The key lock on these chests is a privacy lock, not theft protection.

items.name: Encrypted USB drive for document copies
items.need: Scans of your key documents on a drive in the bag let you prove identity and file claims anywhere, and encryption means a lost bag does not hand a stranger your identity.
items.how_to_choose: The copies are only safe if the drive is encrypted. A keypad drive unlocks with a PIN on the drive itself, so it works on any computer, phone or library PC without software. If you buy a keypad drive, choose one validated to FIPS 140-3. The free route is an ordinary drive encrypted with the tools built into Windows or macOS, which works well but only opens easily on the same kind of computer.

qty.note: One per household, kept in the bag. A second copy stored somewhere else is wise.

items.already_own: Any working USB drive from a major brand is good enough if you encrypt it with BitLocker To Go (Windows Pro, Enterprise or Education) or as an encrypted volume in macOS Disk Utility. Write the password down somewhere safe that is not in the same bag.
item_flags: A forgotten PIN or password means the data is gone. Hardware-encrypted drives erase themselves after a set number of wrong tries.
Encrypting a drive in macOS Disk Utility erases everything on it first (Apple).

items.name: Radio for the bag
items.need: When phone networks are jammed or down, broadcast radio and NOAA Weather Radio are how official instructions reach you, and a pocket set on AA cells runs for days.
items.how_to_choose: Look for AM, FM and the NOAA weather band, and check what it runs on: AA cells can be bought anywhere and swapped in seconds, while a built-in rechargeable battery has to be kept charged. Store the batteries outside the radio so they cannot leak into it.

items.name: Eye protection
items.need: Dust, ash and falling grit after a collapse, fire or windstorm can blind you long enough to stop you getting out, and sealed eye protection keeps your eyes working.
items.how_to_choose: Look for the ANSI Z87.1 impact marking (Z87+ on the lens). For dust, ash and grit, a foam or rubber gasket that closes the gap around the eyes matters more than lens quality. If you wear prescription glasses, choose goggles made to fit over them. Check that the pair fits with your N95 on. Treat every pick here as protection from dust, debris and impact only, never from gases, fumes or chemical vapors.

qty.note: One per adult, in the bag.

item_flags: The makers sell these for dust, debris and impact. Do not rely on them against toxic gases, fumes or chemical vapors.
